label: B01
question: For one op_name, how do I request a daily total cost and mean latency from POST /calls/stats? Explain granularity and the usage_metrics and call_metrics fields.
answer:
To get a daily total cost and mean latency for one op, send a `POST /calls/stats` request with these fields:

- `granularity: 86400` (one day, in seconds)
- a filter on your op name: `filter.op_names`
- `total_cost` with `sum` in `usage_metrics`
- `latency_ms` with `avg` in `call_metrics`

Only `project_id` and `start` are required. `end` is optional and defaults to now [S1]. The longest time range you can query is 31 days [S2].

```python
import os
import requests

payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",   # inclusive, UTC
    "end": "2026-03-08T00:00:00Z",     # exclusive, optional
    "granularity": 86400,              # one-day buckets
    "filter": {"op_names": ["[YOUR-OP-NAME]"]},
    "usage_metrics": [{"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}],
    "call_metrics": [{"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg"]}],
}
response = requests.post(
    "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats",
    json=payload,
    auth=("api", os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")),
)
print(response.json())
```

The URL and API-key login follow the documented example. That example also sets `trace_roots_only: True` in the filter, which you can add if you only want top-level calls [S2].

**`granularity`**
- It sets the size of each time "bucket" (time window), in seconds. For example, 3600 is one hour and 86400 is one day [S1].
- If you leave it out, Weave picks a size based on your time range. Weave also adjusts it if your setting would create more than 10,000 buckets [S1].
- Buckets line up to `timezone`, which defaults to `UTC`. The response reports the bucket size actually used [S1].

**`usage_metrics`**
- This field covers token and cost metrics: `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `total_tokens`, the cache token counts, `input_cost`, `output_cost` and `total_cost` [S1].
- Each entry has a `metric`, optional `aggregations` (default `sum`) and optional `percentiles` [S1].
- Results come back in `usage_buckets`, grouped by time **and model**. You'll see fields like `sum_total_cost` [S1, S2].
- Because cost is split by model, you need to add up `sum_total_cost` across all model rows with the same `timestamp` to get one daily total. This is my inference from how the buckets are grouped.

**`call_metrics`**
- This field covers per-call metrics: `latency_ms`, `call_count` and `error_count` [S1].
- Available aggregations include `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min` and `max`, and you can also request percentiles [S1, S2].
- Results come back in `call_buckets`, grouped by time only. That gives you one `avg_latency_ms` value per day [S1, S2].

## Export Call metrics

When you need aggregate insights, such as cost or latency trends, rather than the underlying Call records, use the metrics endpoint described in this section.

You can also use the Weave Service API's [POST `/calls/stats` endpoint](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-stats) to retrieve metrics about your Calls without retrieving the Call data itself. You can retrieve information about your Calls, such as latency and cost, and aggregate them by sum, average, minimum, maximum, and count. For example, you can retrieve:

* Total token usage
* Average latency
* Maximum tokens used
* Total cost
* Minimum input tokens

The endpoint provides several filtering options so you can target Calls made within specified times, and by other properties, such as:

* Op name
* Trace ID
* Thread ID
* User ID

The following example demonstrates how to retrieve Calls generated from an Op named `web_app` over two days. Replace `[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]` with your team and project names:

```python Python lines {10-11,16-24} theme={"system"}
import requests
import json
import os

url = "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats"

payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",
# Specify the size of the buckets, in seconds.
    "granularity": 86400,
    "filter": {
        "trace_roots_only": True,
        "op_names": ["web_app"]
    },
# Specify metrics and their aggregate function
    "usage_metrics": [
        {"metric": "total_tokens", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}
    ],
    "call_metrics": [
        {"metric": "call_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "error_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg", "min", "max"], "percentiles": [50, 95, 99]}
    ]
}

API_KEY = os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")

response = requests.post(url, json=payload, auth=("api", API_KEY))

print(json.dumps(response.json(), indent=2))
```

  },
// Specify metrics and their aggregate function
  usage_metrics: [
    { metric: "total_tokens", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "total_cost", aggregations: ["sum"] },
  ],
  call_metrics: [
    { metric: "call_count", aggregations: ["sum"] },

  ],
};

const API_KEY = [REDACTED_SECRET];

const response = await fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    Authorization: "[REDACTED_SECRET]" + btoa(`api:${API_KEY}`),
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(payload),
});

const data = await response.json();
console.log(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));
```

The request also specifies how to aggregate the metrics. You can aggregate metrics by `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, and `count`.

* `usage_buckets`: Groups Call metrics for each day by the model used.
* `call_buckets`: Groups Call metrics for each day regardless of the model used.

question: Can Weave show the screenshots that are already in our object storage without uploading another copy? Explain what we log and every required storage and team setup step.
answer:
Yes. Weave can show screenshots that already sit in your own S3 or Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket. You log each screenshot's bucket URI, meaning its address such as `s3://bucket/key`, as a plain string in a trace. Weave sends only the URI to its servers, and the image bytes stay in your bucket [S1]. This is different from the Content API, which reads the bytes and stores a copy in Weave [S1].

**What you log**
- The URI as a string anywhere in a trace: an op's input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name doesn't matter, and you don't need a content annotation [S4, S6]. An "op" is a function you decorate with `@weave.op` so Weave records its calls.
- Only `s3://` and `gs://` URIs work, and only for buckets registered to your team [S4].
- The file extension decides how the file is shown. Common image formats (for example `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and common video formats (for example `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) appear inline. Other formats appear as a download link [S4].

```python
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

@weave.op
def record_screenshot(screenshot_uri: str) -> dict:
    return {"screenshot": screenshot_uri}

record_screenshot("s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/screens/step-001.png")
```
This follows the documented pattern [S6]. For agent applications, there is a separate guide for agent spans [S6].

**Before you start**
- Your deployment must support it: Multi-tenant Cloud, or preview on Dedicated Cloud and Self-Managed v0.84.0+ [S5].
- You need a CoreWeave Forge account with an API key, an S3 or GCS bucket you control with at least one object, and organization admin permission [S5].

**Storage setup (read-only access)**
When someone opens a trace, W&B creates a short-lived download link (a "presigned URL") for each object, so it needs read access to the bucket [S2].
- **S3:** Add a bucket policy that grants `s3:GetObject` to `arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration`. Then add a CORS rule allowing `GET` and `HEAD` from `https://forge.coreweave.com`. CORS is the setting that lets the browser fetch the images. If objects use a customer-managed KMS key, that key's policy must also grant this role `kms:Decrypt` [S2].
- **GCS:** Give `wandb-integration@wandb-production.iam.gserviceaccount.com` the `roles/storage.objectViewer` role, and add the same kind of CORS rule [S2].

**Team setup**
1. Open `https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`, go to **Reference buckets** and select **Add bucket** [S3].
2. Choose AWS or Google Cloud and enter the bucket name without the `s3://` or `gs://` prefix [S3].
3. Enter the key of one existing object, such as `photos/cat.png`. W&B reads it to check access and CORS. After that, links work for any object in the bucket [S3].
4. Optionally select **Test connection**, then select **Add bucket** [S3].

Screenshots won't display until the bucket is registered [S3]. Once it is, they show inline in the **Traces** view. If Weave can't find an object or the bucket isn't registered, you'll see the plain URI instead [S7].

# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in Weave traces by logging their URIs, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.heading: Configure your bucket
sources.text:
## Configure your bucket

Grant W\&B read access to the bucket and allow the browser to fetch objects with CORS.

When you view a trace, W\&B presigns a short-lived download URL for each referenced object. Grant the W\&B integration principal read access on the bucket so presigning can succeed. This is read-only access for inline rendering.

**AWS S3**

1. Apply a bucket policy that grants the W\&B integration principal `s3:GetObject`. Save the following as `bucket-policy.json`, replacing `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your bucket name:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   {
     "Version": "2012-10-17",
     "Id": "WandBAccess",
     "Statement": [{
       "Sid": "WandbAccess",
       "Effect": "Allow",
       "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration"},
       "Action": "s3:GetObject",
       "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::[YOUR-BUCKET]/*"
     }]
   }
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket [YOUR-BUCKET] --policy file://bucket-policy.json
   ```

2. Apply a CORS configuration so the app can fetch objects in the browser. Save the following as `cors.json`:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   {
     "CORSRules": [{
       "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
       "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD"],
       "AllowedOrigins": ["https://forge.coreweave.com"],
       "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"],
       "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
     }]
   }
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   aws s3api put-bucket-cors --bucket [YOUR-BUCKET] --cors-configuration file://cors.json
   ```

> [!NOTE]
>
> If an object is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, its key policy must also grant `arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration` `kms:Decrypt`. The bucket policy alone is not sufficient.

**Google Cloud Storage**

1. Grant the W\&B integration service account `roles/storage.objectViewer` on the bucket. Replace `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your bucket name:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://[YOUR-BUCKET] \
     --member="serviceAccount:wandb-integration@wandb-production.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
     --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
   ```

2. Apply a CORS configuration so the app can fetch objects in the browser. Save the following as `cors.json`:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   [{
     "origin": ["https://forge.coreweave.com"],
     "method": ["GET", "HEAD"],
     "responseHeader": ["ETag"],
     "maxAgeSeconds": 3000
   }]
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   gcloud storage buckets update gs://[YOUR-BUCKET] --cors-file=cors.json
   ```

At this point, Weight & Biases can read objects from your bucket, and the UI can fetch them in the browser.

## Register the reference bucket

Register the bucket in your team settings so Weave can presign and display referenced URIs.

1. Go to your team settings page (`https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`).
2. In the **Reference buckets** section, select **Add bucket**.
3. Select your cloud provider (**AWS** or **Google Cloud**).
4. For the bucket name, enter `[YOUR-BUCKET]` only — without the `s3://` or `gs://` prefix.
5. For the object key, enter the key of an existing object in the bucket, for example `photos/cat.png` (the object key only, not a full URL). W\&B reads this one object to confirm it has read access and that CORS is configured correctly. This checks access only; once verified, presigning works for any object in the bucket.
6. Optionally, select **Test connection** to validate the configuration without saving.
7. Select **Add bucket** to save.

# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in Weave traces by logging their URIs, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.heading: How it works
sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

question: I changed both my assistant's instructions and its model settings. How do I keep those app revisions identifiable in Weave and inspect which individual test answers improved or regressed?
answer:
Put the instructions and model settings into a `weave.Model` class. Then run the same `weave.Evaluation` on the old and new versions, and compare the two runs side by side in the **Compare evaluations** view.

**1. Make each revision identifiable**
- Create a class that inherits from `weave.Model`. Give every field a type, such as `system_prompt`, `model_name` and `temperature`, and add a typed `invoke` or `predict` method decorated with `@weave.op()` [S1].
- When you change a field value or the model's code, Weave records the change and creates a new version. This lets you compare outputs across versions of your app [S1]. Weave doesn't log fields whose names start with an underscore [S1].

**2. Score both versions on the same test set**
- A `weave.Evaluation` holds a dataset of test examples and one or more scorers (functions that grade each answer). Each `.evaluate()` call is one evaluation run [S6, S7].
- You can label each run with `__weave={"display_name": ...}` [S7].

```python
import asyncio
import weave

weave.init("YOUR_PROJECT")

class Assistant(weave.Model):
    system_prompt: str
    model_name: str
    temperature: float

    @weave.op()
    def predict(self, question: str) -> str:
        return "YOUR_LLM_CALL_HERE"

evaluation = weave.Evaluation(
    name="assistant_eval",
    dataset=YOUR_DATASET,
    scorers=[YOUR_SCORER],
)

old = Assistant(system_prompt="OLD_PROMPT", model_name="OLD_MODEL", temperature=0.2)
new = Assistant(system_prompt="NEW_PROMPT", model_name="NEW_MODEL", temperature=0.7)

asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(old, __weave={"display_name": "old-prompt-and-settings"}))
asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(new, __weave={"display_name": "new-prompt-and-settings"}))
```

The `predict` body and the `YOUR_...` names are placeholders. In a notebook, use `await` instead of `asyncio.run` [S6].

**3. See which answers improved or regressed**
1. Open **Evals** in the project sidebar, tick both runs and select **Compare** [S4].
2. The leftmost run is the baseline (the reference the others are measured against). To change it, use the run's action menu and choose **Make baseline** [S5].
3. Open the **Dataset results** tab. Each row is one test example and shows the input, each run's output and its scores. Select a row to see the outputs side by side [S2, S3].
4. When you compare exactly two runs, scatter plots show which examples scored differently. Select a group of points to filter the table, and use **Dimension** to choose the metric [S3].

The per-example table only appears if both runs share dataset rows, so use the same dataset for both [S3]. Note that `weave.Model` is only available in Python [S1].

sources.heading: Use `weave.Model`
sources.text:
## Use `weave.Model`

> [!WARNING]
>
> The `weave.Model` class is only supported in Python.

Using Weave `Model`s means that Weave stores and versions parameters such as model vendor IDs, prompts, temperature, and more when they change.

To create a `Model` in Weave, you need the following:

* A class that inherits from `weave.Model`.
* Type definitions on all class fields.
* A typed `invoke` function with the `@weave.op()` decorator.

When you change the class fields or the code that defines your model, Weave logs these changes and updates the version. This ensures that you can compare the generations across different versions of your app.

In the following example, Weave tracks and versions the model name, temperature, and system prompt:

**Python**

```python lines {26,33-34} theme={"system"}
import json
from openai import OpenAI

import weave

@weave.op()
def extract_dinos(wmodel: weave.Model, sentence: str) -> dict:
    response = wmodel.client.chat.completions.create(
        model=wmodel.model_name,
        temperature=wmodel.temperature,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": wmodel.system_prompt
            },
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": sentence
            }
            ],
            response_format={ "type": "json_object" }
        )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Subclass with a weave.Model
class ExtractDinos(weave.Model):
    client: OpenAI = None
    model_name: str
    temperature: float
    system_prompt: str

    # Ensure your function is called `invoke` or `predict`
    @weave.op()
    def invoke(self, sentence: str) -> dict:
        dino_data  = extract_dinos(self, sentence)
        return json.loads(dino_data)
```

**TypeScript**

```plaintext theme={"system"}
This feature is not available in TypeScript yet.
```

Now you can instantiate and call the model with `invoke`:

**Python**

```python lines {7,18} theme={"system"}
weave.init('jurassic-park')
client = OpenAI()

system_prompt = """Extract any dinosaur `name`, their `common_name`, \
names and whether its `diet` is a herbivore or carnivore, in JSON format."""

dinos = ExtractDinos(
    client=client,
    model_name='gpt-4o',
    temperature=0.4,
    system_prompt=system_prompt
)

sentence = """I watched as a Tyrannosaurus rex (T. rex) chased after a Triceratops (Trike), \
both carnivore and herbivore locked in an ancient dance. Meanwhile, a gentle giant \
Brachiosaurus (Brachi) calmly munched on treetops, blissfully unaware of the chaos below."""

result = dinos.invoke(sentence)
print(result)
```

**TypeScript**

```plaintext theme={"system"}
This feature is not available in TypeScript yet.
```

After calling `.invoke()`, the trace in Weave tracks the model parameters along with the code for the model functions decorated with `weave.op()`. The model is also versioned (`v21` in this case). Click the model to see all the calls that used that version.

![Reusing a weave model](https://mintcdn.com/coreweave-dbfa0e8d/3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx/products/wandb/weave/_media/tutorial-model_invoke3.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx\&q=85\&s=9fdbffd1e5837823322919a24c541e08)

A note on using `weave.Model`:

* You can use `predict` instead of `invoke` for the name of the function in your Weave `Model` if you prefer.
* To track other class methods with Weave, wrap them in `weave.op()`.
* Weave ignores parameters starting with an underscore and doesn't log them.

answer:
The one setup step left is registering the bucket as a **reference bucket** in your team settings. After that, each path just needs to record the picture's `s3://` address as a plain string. ## Register the reference bucket

1. Go to your team settings page (`https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`).

7. Select **Add bucket** to save.

# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in Weave traces by logging their URIs, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.heading: How it works
sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

question: For one op_name, how do I request a daily total cost and mean latency from POST /calls/stats? Explain granularity and the usage_metrics and call_metrics fields.
answer:
To get a daily total cost and mean latency for one op, send `POST /calls/stats` with `granularity: 86400` (one day in seconds). Put the op in `filter.op_names`, ask for `total_cost` with `sum` in `usage_metrics`, and ask for `latency_ms` with `avg` in `call_metrics` [S1, S2].

```python
import os
import requests

payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",
    "end": "2026-03-08T00:00:00Z",
    "granularity": 86400,
    "timezone": "UTC",
    "filter": {"op_names": ["[YOUR-OP-NAME]"]},
    "usage_metrics": [{"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}],
    "call_metrics": [{"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg"]}],
}

response = requests.post(
    "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats",
    json=payload,
    auth=("api", os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")),
)
print(response.json())
```

This follows the documented example, which authenticates with your W&B API key (read here from the `WANDB_API_KEY` environment variable) [S1].

**Time range and `granularity`**
- `project_id` and `start` are required. `start` is included in the range; `end` is excluded and defaults to now [S2].
- `granularity` is the size of each time bucket in seconds. If you leave it out, it's chosen based on your time range. It will be adjusted if it would create more than 10,000 buckets [S2].
- `timezone` sets where bucket boundaries fall, such as midnight in your time zone. It's an IANA name like `America/New_York` and defaults to UTC [S2].
- One request can cover at most 31 days [S1].

**`usage_metrics`** (token and cost totals)
- Choices are input, output, total, cache-read and cache-creation tokens, plus `input_cost`, `output_cost` and `total_cost` [S2].
- Each entry has a `metric`, plus `aggregations` (defaults to `["sum"]`) and optional `percentiles` [S2].
- Results come back in `usage_buckets`, split by day and model, with fields like `sum_total_cost` [S1, S2]. If the op uses several models, my inference is that you add the per-model values for each day to get one daily cost.

**`call_metrics`** (per-call measurements)
- Choices are `latency_ms`, `call_count` and `error_count` [S2]. Aggregations include `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min` and `max` [S1].
- These aren't split by model. Results come back in `call_buckets`, one per day, with fields like `avg_latency_ms` [S1, S2].

The documented example also sets `"trace_roots_only": True` in the filter [S1]. That's optional; add it if you only want calls that start a trace.

## Export Call metrics

When you need aggregate insights, such as cost or latency trends, rather than the underlying Call records, use the metrics endpoint described in this section.

You can also use the Weave Service API's [POST `/calls/stats` endpoint](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/service-api/calls/call-stats) to retrieve metrics about your Calls without retrieving the Call data itself. You can retrieve information about your Calls, such as latency and cost, and aggregate them by sum, average, minimum, maximum, and count. For example, you can retrieve:

* Total token usage
* Average latency
* Maximum tokens used
* Total cost
* Minimum input tokens

The endpoint provides several filtering options so you can target Calls made within specified times, and by other properties, such as:

* Op name
* Trace ID
* Thread ID
* User ID

The following example demonstrates how to retrieve Calls generated from an Op named `web_app` over two days. Replace `[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]` with your team and project names:

```python Python lines {10-11,16-24} theme={"system"}
import requests
import json
import os

url = "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats"

payload = {
    "project_id": "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
    "start": "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",
# Specify the size of the buckets, in seconds.
    "granularity": 86400,
    "filter": {
        "trace_roots_only": True,
        "op_names": ["web_app"]
    },
# Specify metrics and their aggregate function
    "usage_metrics": [
        {"metric": "total_tokens", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "total_cost", "aggregations": ["sum"]}
    ],
    "call_metrics": [
        {"metric": "call_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "error_count", "aggregations": ["sum"]},
        {"metric": "latency_ms", "aggregations": ["avg", "min", "max"], "percentiles": [50, 95, 99]}
    ]
}

API_KEY = os.getenv("WANDB_API_KEY")

response = requests.post(url, json=payload, auth=("api", API_KEY))

print(json.dumps(response.json(), indent=2))
```

```typescript TypeScript lines {6-7,13-20} theme={"system"}
const url = "https://trace.wandb.ai/calls/stats";

const payload = {
  project_id: "[YOUR-TEAM-NAME/YOUR-PROJECT-NAME]",
  start: "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z",
// Specify the size of the buckets, in seconds.
  granularity: 86400,
  filter: {
    trace_roots_only: true,
    op_names: ["web_app"],
  },
// Specify metrics and their aggregate function
  usage_metrics: [
    { metric: "total_tokens", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "total_cost", aggregations: ["sum"] },
  ],
  call_metrics: [
    { metric: "call_count", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "error_count", aggregations: ["sum"] },
    { metric: "latency_ms", aggregations: ["avg", "min", "max"], percentiles: [50, 95, 99] },
  ],
};

const API_KEY = [REDACTED_SECRET];

const response = await fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    Authorization: "[REDACTED_SECRET]" + btoa(`api:${API_KEY}`),
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(payload),
});

const data = await response.json();
console.log(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));
```

The request also specifies how to aggregate the metrics. You can aggregate metrics by `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, and `count`.

The endpoint returns a JSON object. The following example response shows two days' worth of metrics. Each day (bucket) appears as its own object in the `usage_buckets` and `call_buckets` arrays. Each array breaks down the metrics differently:

* `usage_buckets`: Groups Call metrics for each day by the model used.
* `call_buckets`: Groups Call metrics for each day regardless of the model used.

Set the granularity field (in seconds) in the request to change the bucket size.

question: I am adding postprocess_inputs and postprocess_output to a Python @weave.op. What types go into and out of each hook, and which representation is saved in the trace?
answer:
Each hook receives the raw data and returns a changed version, and Weave saves the changed version in the trace. The docs say the hooks let you change the data Weave logs without modifying the original function [S1].

**`postprocess_inputs`**
- **Receives:** a `dict` whose keys are the argument names and whose values are the argument values. For example, `func(a=1, hide_me="password123")` gives `{"a": 1, "hide_me": "password123"}` [S1].
- **Returns:** a `dict` of the changed inputs, such as the same dict without `hide_me`. The docs example uses the type hints `dict[str, Any] -> dict[str, Any]` [S1].

**`postprocess_output`**
- **Receives:** whatever value your function would normally return [S1].
- **Returns:** the changed output. In the docs example, the hook takes a `CustomObject` and returns a new `CustomObject` with `secret_password="REDACTED"` [S1]. Keeping the same type is just the pattern the example uses.

**Which version is saved in the trace**
- The trace stores the **changed** versions: the dict from `postprocess_inputs` and the value from `postprocess_output`. Removing or redacting sensitive data from logs is the documented purpose [S1, S2].
- **Not confirmed:** whether your function and its caller still see the original, unchanged values. S1's wording ("without modifying the original function") suggests they do, but that's my inference. The PII guide also says the hooks can modify "the data that is passed to your LLM call or logged to Weave" [S2]. If this matters for your code, test it before relying on it.

```python
from typing import Any
import weave

def postprocess_inputs(inputs: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {k: v for k, v in inputs.items() if k != "hide_me"}

def postprocess_output(output: Any) -> Any:
    return "REDACTED"  # placeholder transformation

@weave.op(postprocess_inputs=postprocess_inputs, postprocess_output=postprocess_output)
def func(a: int, hide_me: str) -> str:
    return hide_me

weave.init("your-project-name")
func(a=1, hide_me="password123")
```

The docs examples call `weave.init(...)` before calling the op. Without it, the op runs as a normal function and nothing is traced [S1]. This feature is not yet available in TypeScript [S1].

question: Our nightly test must keep using the wording we published last Friday even when teammates publish edits under the same prompt name. How can we retrieve that particular revision reliably?
answer:
Pin your test to that exact version instead of the prompt name alone. Every `weave.publish` call creates a version that can't be changed afterward. When teammates publish new content under the same name, Weave adds new versions and keeps the older ones [S2, S8]. So a ref (a pointer to a stored object) that names last Friday's version will keep loading that wording.

**Steps**

1. **Find Friday's version.** In the Weave project sidebar, open **Assets → Prompts**. Click **(x) Versions** for your prompt to list every version. To confirm you have the right wording, tick two versions and click **Compare** to see the differences [S7].
2. **Note its version hash or index.** A version can be identified by its hash or by an index like `v3` [S4].
3. **Load it in the test** with `weave.ref("<name>:<version>").get()`. This form requires calling `weave.init(...)` first [S1]:

```python
import weave

weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")

# Use the version hash or index of last Friday's version, not :latest
prompt = weave.ref("your_prompt_name:<friday_version_hash_or_index>").get()
```

You can also use the full URI, `weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<prompt_name>:<version>`, which doesn't require `weave.init(...)` [S1, S4].

**What to avoid**
- **A bare name or `:latest`.** `weave.ref(<name>)` loads the `:latest` version, so your test would pick up teammates' edits [S1].
- **Movable aliases** (named labels like `production`). An alias can be moved to a different version at any time [S6], and everything that uses it then picks up the change automatically [S5]. That suits production rollouts, but a test that must never change is better pinned to a specific version.

sources.text:
## Retrieve a prompt version in code

To retrieve a prompt, create a reference to its name and version, then call `.get()` to load it. A ref points to a stored object; `.get()` fetches that object so you can use it in your application.

You can construct refs with a few different styles:

* `weave.ref(<name>)`: Retrieves the `:latest` version of a prompt. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<name>:<alias_or_version>)`: Retrieves a prompt by alias, version hash, or version index. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<fully_qualified_ref_uri>)`: Retrieves the prompt located at the specified [fully qualified ref URI](#construct-a-fully-qualified-ref-uri). Does not require calling `weave.init(...)`.

The following example loads the `support_prompt:v3` version so you can use it in your application:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")

prompt = weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get()
```

## Construct a fully qualified ref URI

Before retrieving a prompt version in code, it helps to understand how Weave identifies stored objects. A fully qualified ref URI uniquely identifies a Weave object.

A fully qualified Weave object ref URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<object_name>:<object_version>
```

* `your-team-name`: Weights & Biases entity (username or team name)
* `your-project-name`: Weights & Biases project
* `object_name`: object name
* `object_version`: either a version hash, a version index like `v0` or `v1`, or an alias like `:latest` or `:production`. All objects have the `:latest` alias.

For example, a fully qualified Weave prompt URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///your-team-name/your-project-name/object/support_prompt:v3
```

## Use prompts in production

When deploying prompts in production systems, use an [alias](#add-prompt-tags-and-aliases) like `production` rather than a version index or the latest version. In your production application, load the prompt with `weave.ref(<name>:<alias>).get()`.

Using an alias keeps production behavior stable and predictable. When you're ready to promote a new version, move the alias to that version. All consumers then automatically pick up the change.

A common workflow looks like this:

1. Develop and test a new prompt version.
2. Evaluate the new prompt against datasets or evaluation suites.
3. Move the `production` alias to the new version with `client.set_aliases(new_ref, "production")`.

This approach lets teams safely iterate on prompts without unexpectedly changing production behavior.

sources.heading: How prompt versions are created
sources.text:
## How prompt versions are created

Weave automatically tracks every version of your prompts, creating a complete history of how your prompts evolve. This versioning system is important for prompt engineering workflows. It lets you experiment safely, track what changes improved or hurt performance, and roll back to previous versions if needed. Each time you publish a prompt with the same name but different content, Weave creates a new version while preserving all previous versions.

Each version is immutable. Once created, the contents of that version cannot be changed. If you update a prompt and publish it again, Weave creates a new version while preserving previous versions.

Versioning enables you to:

* Reproduce past experiments.
* Safely iterate on prompt changes.
* Roll out prompt updates in a controlled way.

sources.text:
## Retrieve a prompt version in code

To retrieve a prompt, create a reference to its name and version, then call `.get()` to load it. A ref points to a stored object; `.get()` fetches that object so you can use it in your application.

You can construct refs with a few different styles:

* `weave.ref(<name>)`: Retrieves the `:latest` version of a prompt. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<name>:<alias_or_version>)`: Retrieves a prompt by alias, version hash, or version index. Requires calling `weave.init(...)`.
* `weave.ref(<fully_qualified_ref_uri>)`: Retrieves the prompt located at the specified [fully qualified ref URI](#construct-a-fully-qualified-ref-uri). Does not require calling `weave.init(...)`.

The following example loads the `support_prompt:v3` version so you can use it in your application:

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave

weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")

prompt = weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get()
```

## Construct a fully qualified ref URI

Before retrieving a prompt version in code, it helps to understand how Weave identifies stored objects. A fully qualified ref URI uniquely identifies a Weave object.

A fully qualified Weave object ref URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///<your-team-name>/<your-project-name>/object/<object_name>:<object_version>

* `your-project-name`: Weights & Biases project
* `object_name`: object name
* `object_version`: either a version hash, a version index like `v0` or `v1`, or an alias like `:latest` or `:production`. All objects have the `:latest` alias.

For example, a fully qualified Weave prompt URI looks like this:

```text theme={"system"}
weave:///your-team-name/your-project-name/object/support_prompt:v3
```

## Use prompts in production

When deploying prompts in production systems, use an [alias](#add-prompt-tags-and-aliases) like `production` rather than a version index or the latest version. In your production application, load the prompt with `weave.ref(<name>:<alias>).get()`.

2. Evaluate the new prompt against datasets or evaluation suites.
3. Move the `production` alias to the new version with `client.set_aliases(new_ref, "production")`.

This approach lets teams safely iterate on prompts without unexpectedly changing production behavior.

question: Can Weave show the screenshots that are already in our object storage without uploading another copy? Explain what we log and every required storage and team setup step.
answer:
Yes. Weave can show screenshots that are already in your own S3 or Google Cloud Storage bucket without uploading them again. This feature is called reference media, or BYOB ("bring your own bucket"). You log each screenshot's bucket address (its URI) as an ordinary string, and Weave displays the image from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the image stays in your bucket [S1].

**What you log**
- Put a string such as `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png` anywhere in a trace: an Op's input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name doesn't matter [S2]. You don't need a `Content` annotation [S6].
- When you open the trace, Weave turns the URI into a short-lived signed download link (a presigned URL) and shows the image in place. The file extension decides how it's shown: `.png`, `.jpg` and `.gif` appear as images, `.mp4`, `.mov` and `.webm` as video, and other formats as a download link. Only `s3://` and `gs://` URIs that point to a bucket registered for your team are resolved [S2].
- Don't use the Content API for this: it reads the image and stores a copy in Weave [S1].

```python
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

@weave.op
def describe_screenshot(image_uri: str) -> dict:
    return {"image": image_uri}

describe_screenshot("s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/screenshots/step1.png")
```
This is adapted from the documented example [S6]. If your app is an agent, there's a separate guide for agent spans [S6].

**Before you start** [S3]
- Hosting: available in W&B Multi-tenant Cloud. Dedicated Cloud and Self-Managed v0.84.0+ have it in preview.
- A CoreWeave Forge account and API key.
- An S3 or GCS bucket you control that holds at least one object.
- Organization admin permission. Adding a reference bucket needs the same permission as creating a team.

**Storage setup** (read-only access) [S4]
- **AWS S3:** Add a bucket policy that grants `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::[YOUR-BUCKET]/*` to `arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration`. Then add a browser-access (CORS) rule that allows `GET` and `HEAD` from `https://forge.coreweave.com` and exposes the `ETag` header. If your objects are encrypted with your own KMS key, the key policy must also give that role `kms:Decrypt`.
- **GCS:** Grant `roles/storage.objectViewer` to `wandb-integration@wandb-production.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. Then add a CORS rule with the same origin, methods and `ETag` header.

**Team setup** [S5]
1. Open `https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`.
2. In **Reference buckets**, select **Add bucket** and choose **AWS** or **Google Cloud**.
3. Enter the bucket name without the `s3://` or `gs://` prefix.
4. Enter the key of one existing object, such as `photos/cat.png`. W&B reads it once to check access and CORS. After that check passes, any object in the bucket can be shown.
5. Optionally select **Test connection**, then select **Add bucket**.

Your screenshot URIs won't display until the bucket is registered [S5]. Reference buckets are set up per team, so each team that needs to see the screenshots must register the bucket [S1].

# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in Weave traces by logging their URIs, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

sources.heading: Configure your bucket
sources.text:
## Configure your bucket

Grant W\&B read access to the bucket and allow the browser to fetch objects with CORS.

When you view a trace, W\&B presigns a short-lived download URL for each referenced object. Grant the W\&B integration principal read access on the bucket so presigning can succeed. This is read-only access for inline rendering.

**AWS S3**

1. Apply a bucket policy that grants the W\&B integration principal `s3:GetObject`. Save the following as `bucket-policy.json`, replacing `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your bucket name:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   {
     "Version": "2012-10-17",
     "Id": "WandBAccess",
     "Statement": [{
       "Sid": "WandbAccess",
       "Effect": "Allow",
       "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration"},
       "Action": "s3:GetObject",
       "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::[YOUR-BUCKET]/*"
     }]
   }
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket [YOUR-BUCKET] --policy file://bucket-policy.json
   ```

2. Apply a CORS configuration so the app can fetch objects in the browser. Save the following as `cors.json`:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   {
     "CORSRules": [{
       "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
       "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD"],
       "AllowedOrigins": ["https://forge.coreweave.com"],
       "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"],
       "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
     }]
   }
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   aws s3api put-bucket-cors --bucket [YOUR-BUCKET] --cors-configuration file://cors.json
   ```

> [!NOTE]
>
> If an object is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, its key policy must also grant `arn:aws:iam::725579432336:role/WandbIntegration` `kms:Decrypt`. The bucket policy alone is not sufficient.

**Google Cloud Storage**

1. Grant the W\&B integration service account `roles/storage.objectViewer` on the bucket. Replace `[YOUR-BUCKET]` with your bucket name:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://[YOUR-BUCKET] \
     --member="serviceAccount:wandb-integration@wandb-production.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
     --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
   ```

2. Apply a CORS configuration so the app can fetch objects in the browser. Save the following as `cors.json`:

   ```json lines theme={"system"}
   [{
     "origin": ["https://forge.coreweave.com"],
     "method": ["GET", "HEAD"],
     "responseHeader": ["ETag"],
     "maxAgeSeconds": 3000
   }]
   ```

   Then apply it to your bucket:

   ```bash theme={"system"}
   gcloud storage buckets update gs://[YOUR-BUCKET] --cors-file=cors.json
   ```

At this point, Weight & Biases can read objects from your bucket, and the UI can fetch them in the browser.

question: I changed both my assistant's instructions and its model settings. How do I keep those app revisions identifiable in Weave and inspect which individual test answers improved or regressed?
answer:
Put the instructions and model settings in a Python `weave.Model`. Weave versions the model automatically when either changes. Then run the same `Evaluation` (a reusable test setup) on the old and new versions, and compare the two runs in the **Compare evaluations** view. Its **Dataset results** tab shows how each test answer scored in each version.

**1. Keep revisions identifiable**
- Create a class that inherits from `weave.Model`. Give every field a type, and add a typed `invoke` (or `predict`) method decorated with `@weave.op()` [S1].
- Store the system prompt, model name and temperature as class fields. When those fields or the model code change, Weave logs the change and creates a new model version. Each traced call shows the parameters and code, and you can click a model version to see all calls that used it [S1].
- Weave ignores fields whose names start with `_` and doesn't log them. Don't use that prefix for settings you want versioned [S1]. `weave.Model` is Python-only [S1].

```python
import weave

class Assistant(weave.Model):
    model_name: str
    temperature: float
    system_prompt: str

    @weave.op()
    def predict(self, question: str) -> str:
        return "<call your LLM using self.model_name, self.temperature, self.system_prompt>"
```

**2. Score each version on the same tests**
- An `Evaluation` combines test examples (a dataset) with scoring functions. Each call to `.evaluate()` creates a separate evaluation run [S6].
- Run it once on each version, e.g. `asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(model))` [S6].

**3. Find which answers improved or regressed**
1. In the project sidebar, select **Evals**. Tick the checkboxes for the two runs, then select **Compare** [S4].

sources.heading: Use `weave.Model`
sources.text:
## Use `weave.Model`

> [!WARNING]
>
> The `weave.Model` class is only supported in Python.

Using Weave `Model`s means that Weave stores and versions parameters such as model vendor IDs, prompts, temperature, and more when they change.

To create a `Model` in Weave, you need the following:

* A class that inherits from `weave.Model`.
* Type definitions on all class fields.
* A typed `invoke` function with the `@weave.op()` decorator.

When you change the class fields or the code that defines your model, Weave logs these changes and updates the version. This ensures that you can compare the generations across different versions of your app.

In the following example, Weave tracks and versions the model name, temperature, and system prompt:

**Python**

```python lines {26,33-34} theme={"system"}
import json
from openai import OpenAI

import weave

@weave.op()
def extract_dinos(wmodel: weave.Model, sentence: str) -> dict:
    response = wmodel.client.chat.completions.create(
        model=wmodel.model_name,
        temperature=wmodel.temperature,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": wmodel.system_prompt
            },
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": sentence
            }
            ],
            response_format={ "type": "json_object" }
        )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Subclass with a weave.Model
class ExtractDinos(weave.Model):
    client: OpenAI = None
    model_name: str
    temperature: float
    system_prompt: str

    # Ensure your function is called `invoke` or `predict`
    @weave.op()
    def invoke(self, sentence: str) -> dict:
        dino_data  = extract_dinos(self, sentence)
        return json.loads(dino_data)
```

**TypeScript**

```plaintext theme={"system"}
This feature is not available in TypeScript yet.
```

Now you can instantiate and call the model with `invoke`:

**Python**

```python lines {7,18} theme={"system"}
weave.init('jurassic-park')
client = OpenAI()

system_prompt = """Extract any dinosaur `name`, their `common_name`, \
names and whether its `diet` is a herbivore or carnivore, in JSON format."""

dinos = ExtractDinos(
    client=client,
    model_name='gpt-4o',
    temperature=0.4,
    system_prompt=system_prompt
)

sentence = """I watched as a Tyrannosaurus rex (T. rex) chased after a Triceratops (Trike), \
both carnivore and herbivore locked in an ancient dance. Meanwhile, a gentle giant \
Brachiosaurus (Brachi) calmly munched on treetops, blissfully unaware of the chaos below."""

result = dinos.invoke(sentence)
print(result)
```

**TypeScript**

```plaintext theme={"system"}
This feature is not available in TypeScript yet.
```

After calling `.invoke()`, the trace in Weave tracks the model parameters along with the code for the model functions decorated with `weave.op()`. The model is also versioned (`v21` in this case). Click the model to see all the calls that used that version.

![Reusing a weave model](https://mintcdn.com/coreweave-dbfa0e8d/3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx/products/wandb/weave/_media/tutorial-model_invoke3.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx\&q=85\&s=9fdbffd1e5837823322919a24c541e08)

A note on using `weave.Model`:

* You can use `predict` instead of `invoke` for the name of the function in your Weave `Model` if you prefer.
* To track other class methods with Weave, wrap them in `weave.op()`.
* Weave ignores parameters starting with an underscore and doesn't log them.

question: The pictures are already in S3, bucket permissions and CORS are set, and I trace both regular Python functions and an agent's tools. What setup remains, and what should each path record to display those pictures in Weave?
answer:
The main step left is to **register the bucket as a reference bucket for your team** in Weave. After that, each path only needs to record the picture's `s3://` URI as a plain string. Weave doesn't upload the image. When you open a trace, it creates a short-lived signed download link and shows the picture from your bucket [S1, S7].

**Remaining setup**
- Make sure you have organization admin permission. Adding a reference bucket needs the same permission as creating a team. The feature works in Multi-tenant Cloud. It's in preview for Dedicated Cloud and for Self-Managed v0.84.0+ [S6].
- Go to `https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`, open **Reference buckets**, then select **Add bucket**. Choose **AWS** and enter just the bucket name, without `s3://` [S3].
- Enter the key of one object that's already in the bucket, such as `photos/cat.png`. W&B reads that object to confirm it can read the bucket and that CORS is set up correctly. You can select **Test connection** to check without saving. Then select **Add bucket** [S3].
- Until the bucket is registered, the URIs won't render as pictures. Weave only resolves URIs in buckets registered for your team [S3, S7].

**What each path should record**
- **Regular Python functions (`@weave.op`):** Put the URI string, such as `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/photos/cat.png`, in any input or output field. The field name doesn't matter, and you don't need to mark the field as media [S4, S7]. You'll see the pictures in Weave Traces.
- **Agent tools:** Inside `weave.start_conversation` → `weave.start_turn` → `weave.start_tool`, set `tool.result` to the URI string. The picture appears in the **Agents** view, on the tool call that returned it [S5, S8].

The file extension decides how the URI displays. Common image types such as `.png`, `.jpg` and `.gif` show inline. Formats Weave doesn't display inline appear as a download link [S7]. If Weave can't resolve a URI, for example because the object is missing or the bucket isn't registered, the agent view shows the plain URI text instead [S8].

sources.text:
# Reference media in your own bucket (BYOB) using Weave Op

> Render images and video that live in your own cloud bucket in Weave traces by logging their URIs, without importing the bytes into Weave.

Use this technique when the media you want to see in Weave already lives in your own bucket:

* Frames from a video pipeline.
* Screenshots from a browser agent.
* Images a model wrote to S3.

Instead of re-uploading those bytes into Weave, you log the object's URI as a string and Weave renders the image or video inline from your bucket. Only the URI is sent to Weave; the bytes stay in your bucket. Logging a 2 GB video costs the same as logging its path.

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.

sources.heading: How it works
sources.text:
## How it works

Reference media rendering works in three steps:

1. You store a media object in your bucket, for example `s3://[YOUR-BUCKET]/frames/000123.png`.
2. You log that URI as a string value anywhere in a trace: an Op input or output, or an agent tool result. The field name does not matter.
3. When you open the trace, Weave resolves the URI to a short-lived [presigned URL](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/presigned-urls.md) and renders it inline. The file extension decides how it renders. Common image formats (such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.gif`) and video formats (such as `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.webm`) render inline. Other formats render as a download link.

Weave only resolves URIs that point at a bucket registered for your team. Supported schemes are `s3://` and `gs://`.

## Register the reference bucket

Register the bucket in your team settings so Weave can presign and display referenced URIs.

1. Go to your team settings page (`https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/[YOUR-TEAM]/settings`).

This is different from logging media with the [Content API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/media.md#contents-api), which reads the bytes and stores them in Weave.

> [!NOTE]
>
> This is a Weave feature and is separate from [platform BYOB (secure storage connector)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/platform/hosting/data-security/secure-storage-connector.md), which backs W\&B artifact and run storage. Reference media buckets are configured per team and only need read access.
